name: Sun
summary: The G-type star at the centre of our Solar System.
discovery: Known since antiquity
composition: About 73% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass

name: Mercury
summary: Smallest planet and the closest to the Sun.
discovery: Known since antiquity
composition: Rocky planet with a large metallic core

name: Venus
summary: Rocky planet wrapped in a thick, heat-trapping atmosphere.
discovery: Known since antiquity
composition: Rocky planet; atmosphere mostly carbon dioxide

name: Earth
summary: Our home world and the only place known to harbour life.
discovery: Known since antiquity
composition: Rocky planet: iron-nickel core, silicate mantle and crust

name: Mars
summary: Cold desert planet with the tallest volcano in the Solar System.
discovery: Known since antiquity
composition: Rocky planet; thin carbon dioxide atmosphere

name: Jupiter
summary: Largest planet; a gas giant with a Great Red Spot storm.
discovery: Known since antiquity
composition: Mostly hydrogen and helium

name: Saturn
summary: Gas giant best known for its extensive ring system.
discovery: Known since antiquity
composition: Mostly hydrogen and helium

name: Uranus
summary: Ice giant that rotates on its side.
discovery: Discovered 13 March 1781 by William Herschel
composition: Hydrogen and helium over icy materials (water, ammonia, methane)

name: Neptune
summary: Distant ice giant with supersonic winds.
discovery: Identified 23 September 1846 by Johann Galle, from predictions by Urbain Le Verrier (John Couch Adams made independent predictions)
composition: Hydrogen and helium over icy materials (water, ammonia, methane)

name: Moon
summary: Earth's only natural satellite.
discovery: Known since antiquity
composition: Rocky: silicate crust and mantle, small iron core

name: Ceres
summary: Largest object in the main asteroid belt, classified as a dwarf planet.
discovery: Discovered 1 January 1801 by Giuseppe Piazzi
composition: Mixture of rock and water ice

name: Halley's Comet
summary: Famous periodic comet visible from Earth about every 76 years.
discovery: Observed since at least 240 BCE; its return was predicted by Edmond Halley (1705)
composition: Ice, dust and rock (comet nucleus)

name: Milky Way
summary: The barred spiral galaxy that contains our Solar System.

name: Andromeda Galaxy
summary: Nearest large spiral galaxy to the Milky Way (M31).
discovery: Recorded by the Persian astronomer Al-Sufi around 964 CE; shown to lie outside the Milky Way by Edwin Hubble in the 1920s

name: Orion Nebula
summary: Bright star-forming nebula in Orion's sword (M42).

name: Crab Nebula
summary: Supernova remnant in Taurus from a star observed exploding in 1054 CE (M1).
discovery: Supernova recorded in 1054 CE; first catalogued as M1 by Charles Messier (1758)

name: Sagittarius A*
summary: Supermassive black hole at the centre of the Milky Way.

sources.label: GRAVITY Collaboration 2022, Astronomy & Astrophysics: stellar orbits around Sgr A*

discovery: Compact radio source Sagittarius A* discovered in 1974 (Bruce Balick and Robert Brown)

name: M87*
summary: Supermassive black hole in galaxy M87, the first ever imaged (2019, Event Horizon Telescope).

sources.label: Physics World report of the Event Horizon Telescope result (April 2019)

discovery: First black hole imaged: Event Horizon Telescope results published in April 2019

name: Proxima Centauri b
summary: Exoplanet orbiting Proxima Centauri, the closest known star to the Sun.
discovery: Announced in August 2016 (ESO Pale Red Dot campaign)

name: TRAPPIST-1 e
summary: Rocky exoplanet in the TRAPPIST-1 system, in the star's habitable zone.
discovery: Announced in February 2017 with the TRAPPIST-1 system (Gillon et al.)

name: Solar System
summary: The Sun and everything bound to it: eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets.
distance: about 26,000 light-years from the Milky Way's centre

discovery: Described by Giovanni Battista Hodierna before 1654; catalogued by Charles Messier in 1764
name: Triangulum Galaxy
summary: Third-largest galaxy of the Local Group, after Andromeda and the Milky Way (M33).

discovery: Known since antiquity to observers in the Southern Hemisphere
name: Large Magellanic Cloud
summary: Satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, visible to the naked eye from the Southern Hemisphere.

discovery: Discovered by Jean-Philippe de Chéseaux in 1745-46; catalogued by Charles Messier in 1764
name: Eagle Nebula
summary: Star-forming nebula in Serpens containing the Pillars of Creation (M16).

discovery: X-ray source detected in 1964 by a rocket-borne instrument
name: Cygnus X-1
summary: One of the first strong black hole candidates, a stellar-mass black hole in a binary system.

sources.label: Miller-Jones et al. 2021, Science (arXiv 2102.09091): Cygnus X-1 contains a 21-solar mass black hole

discovery: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, 1995
name: 51 Pegasi b
summary: First exoplanet confirmed around a Sun-like star.

discovery: Known since antiquity; its white dwarf companion Sirius B was first observed by Alvan Graham Clark in 1862
name: Sirius
summary: Brightest star in Earth's night sky, a binary system in Canis Major.

discovery: Clyde Tombaugh, Lowell Observatory, 1930
name: Pluto
summary: Dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt, reclassified from planet in 2006.
distance: about 39.5 AU from the Sun on average (about 5.9 billion km)

name: Eris
summary: One of the five dwarf planets the IAU has recognised, with a very small moon called Dysnomia.
composition: Most likely a rocky surface similar to Pluto's; internal structure largely unknown
discovery: Announced 5 Jan 2005, from Palomar Observatory survey data of 21 Oct 2003 (Mike Brown, Chad Trujillo, David Rabinowitz)

name: Haumea
summary: Oval, football-shaped dwarf planet that spins about once every 4 hours, with two known moons: Namaka and Hi'iaka.
composition: Believed to be rock with a coating of ice; surface little known
discovery: Disputed: two teams claim credit (observations from 2003 and 2004); the listed discovery site is Sierra Nevada Observatory, Spain, 7 Mar 2003, with no official discoverer

name: Makemake
summary: Reddish-brown dwarf planet slightly smaller than Pluto, with one provisional moon nicknamed MK 2.
composition: Frozen methane and ethane detected on its surface
discovery: First observed in March 2005 by M.E. Brown, C.A. Trujillo and D.L. Rabinowitz at Palomar Observatory

name: Vesta
summary: Second most massive body in the main asteroid belt; NASA's Dawn spacecraft orbited it from July 2011 to September 2012.
mass: almost 9% of the combined mass of all asteroids
composition: Separated into crust, mantle and core, unlike most known asteroids
discovery: Discovered at Bremen, Germany, on 29 Mar 1807 by Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers

name: Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko
summary: Comet studied up close by ESA's Rosetta, which rendezvoused with it in August 2014 and ended its mission with a controlled impact on 30 Sep 2016.
distance: closest approach to the Sun about 1.3 AU since 1959
composition: Nucleus thought to be quite porous, with a density much lower than water; Rosetta found exposed water ice, glycine and phosphorus
discovery: Discovered 22 Oct 1969 at Alma-Ata Observatory, Russia, by Klim Churyumov examining a photographic plate

name: Main asteroid belt
summary: Region between Mars and Jupiter where most asteroids orbit; the combined mass of all asteroids is less than that of Earth's Moon.
composition: Three broad classes: C-type (chondrite, most common), S-type (silicates and nickel-iron) and M-type (metallic nickel-iron)
caveat: Observed: the belt is estimated to hold between 1.1 and 1.9 million asteroids larger than 1 km (an estimate, not a count). The belt's edges in AU are not given by the cited NASA page, so none are shown.

name: Kuiper Belt
summary: Doughnut-shaped region of icy bodies beyond Neptune; more than 2,000 trans-Neptunian objects have been cataloged.
distance: inner edge about 30 AU (Neptune's orbit); main region ends around 50 AU
composition: Rock, water ice and other frozen compounds
caveat: Individual objects are observed; the region's boundaries and total population are estimates. NASA describes the main region as about 30 to 50 AU, with scattered and detached objects reaching much farther. Not drawn to scale in this site.

name: Oort Cloud
summary: A theorized, thick bubble of distant icy debris surrounding the solar system.
distance: inner edge thought to be 2,000 to 5,000 AU from the Sun; outer edge somewhere between 10,000 and 100,000 AU
composition: Icy debris; planetesimals formed from the same material as the planets
caveat: THEORETICAL: the Oort Cloud has not been mapped. Its size, shape and the hundreds of billions to trillions of bodies NASA says it may contain are model-based, not observed. Any drawing of it is conceptual.

name: Voyager 1
summary: Exited the heliosphere on 25 Aug 2012 and entered interstellar space; flew past Jupiter (5 Mar 1979) and Saturn (12 Nov 1980). NASA lists it as an Active Mission (Extended Mission).
distance: 164.7 AU from Earth on 21 Aug 2024; 17.0 km/s relative to the Sun on that date (NASA's latest stated figures)
discovery: 5 Sep 1977, 12:56:01 UT, Titan IIIE-Centaur from Cape Canaveral, Launch Complex 41
caveat: Figures are NASA's stated values for the date given on its page, not live. NASA's page gives conflicting counts of working science instruments (four in one passage, two in another), so no count is stated here.

name: Voyager 2
summary: The only spacecraft to visit all four giant planets: Jupiter (9 Jul 1979), Saturn (25 Aug 1981 in NASA's table), Uranus (24 Jan 1986) and Neptune (25 Aug 1989). Entered interstellar space in Nov or Dec 2018.
distance: 116.167 AU from Earth on 5 Nov 2017 (about 17.378 billion km); 15.4 km/s relative to the Sun (date not given)
discovery: 20 Aug 1977, 14:29:44 UT, Titan IIIE-Centaur from Cape Canaveral, Launch Complex 41
caveat: Figures are NASA's stated values for the date given on its page, not live. NASA's page contradicts itself on two dates: interstellar entry is 25 Nov 2018 in its key-dates table but 10 Dec 2018 in its text, and Saturn closest approach is 25 Aug 1981 in the table but 01:21 UT on 26 Aug in the text. Both are shown or flagged rather than choosing one silently.

name: James Webb Space Telescope
summary: Joint NASA/ESA/CSA space telescope with a large, segmented, gold-coated mirror that observes the sky in the near- and mid-infrared. NASA lists it as an Active Mission.
distance: orbits the Sun about 1.5 million km (1 million miles) from Earth, at the second Lagrange point (L2)
discovery: 25 Dec 2021, from ESA's launch facility in French Guiana

sources.label: NASA Science: James Webb Space Telescope

caveat: The launch vehicle, mirror diameter and exact wavelength range are not stated on the NASA page used, so they are not given here.

name: Hubble Space Telescope
summary: Space telescope launched and deployed by space shuttle Discovery in 1990, sensitive to ultraviolet through infrared light (115 to 2500 nm), with a 2.4 m primary mirror. Five astronaut servicing missions visited it.
distance: orbits about 483 km (300 miles) above Earth's surface, inclined 28.5 degrees to the equator
discovery: 1990, deployed by space shuttle Discovery (exact date not on the NASA page used)
caveat: NASA's page has no mission-status label; it says Hubble has made observations for more than 36 years and will continue for years to come.

name: Parker Solar Probe
summary: Mission to trace the flow of energy, study the heating of the solar corona and explore what accelerates the solar wind. NASA lists it as Primary Mission in Progress.
distance: closest approach about 6.2 million km (3.9 million miles) from the Sun; about 700,000 km/h (430,000 mph) at closest approach
discovery: 12 Aug 2018, 7:31 UTC, Delta IV-Heavy from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, Florida
caveat: Figures are NASA's stated values for the date given on its page, not live. NASA's page states the closest-approach distance two ways: about 6.2 million km from the Sun, and elsewhere about 6.5 million km from the Sun's surface. Both come from NASA; they are not reconciled here.

name: New Horizons
summary: Flew past Pluto on 14 Jul 2015 (11:49 UT) and past Arrokoth on 1 Jan 2019, which NASA calls the most distant target in history. NASA lists it as an Active Mission.
distance: 60 times as far from the Sun as Earth is, on 1 Oct 2024 (NASA's latest stated figure)
discovery: 19 Jan 2006, 19:00:00 UT, Atlas V 551 from Cape Canaveral, Launch Complex 41
caveat: Figures are NASA's stated values for the date given on its page, not live. NASA's page gives two different Pluto closest-approach distances (about 7,800 km in the text, 12,500 km in a caption), so none is stated here.

name: International Space Station
summary: Crewed space station in low Earth orbit. Construction began in November 1998 and the first crew arrived in October 2000.
distance: about 400 km (200 nautical miles) above Earth
discovery: Construction began November 1998; first crew members arrived October 2000
caveat: Speed, mass, size and the exact first-module date are not on the NASA page used, so they are not given here. The orbit changes slightly over time.

name: Crab Pulsar
summary: The neutron star at the very center of the Crab Nebula. NASA calls it the archetype of the rapidly spinning neutron stars known as pulsars.
distance: the Crab Nebula is 6,500 light-years away, in the constellation Taurus
mass: about the same mass as the Sun
composition: A neutron star: a very dense, highly magnetic remnant of a collapsed star
discovery: The Crab supernova was recorded by Chinese astronomers in 1054 A.D.

sources.label: NASA Science: Hubble captures the beating heart of the Crab Nebula

caveat: Observed, as NASA states it in rounded words. NASA's page gives no spin period, exact size or separate distance for the pulsar itself (the distance is the nebula's), and none is added here.

name: PSR J1748-2446ad
summary: NASA's neutron-star page calls it the fastest known pulsar.

sources.label: NASA Science: Neutron Stars Are Weird!

caveat: NASA's page gives only this spin rate. Its position, distance, mass and discovery are not stated there, so none are given here. 'Fastest known' is NASA's wording as of the page's Aug 2026 update.

name: 3C 273
summary: The first quasar ever identified, found in the early 1960s by astronomer Allan Sandage. It lies in Virgo, is powered by a huge disc of particles around a supermassive black hole, and NASA says it is the brightest of these quasars in our skies. Its jet measures some 200,000 light-years.
distance: its light has taken some 2.5 billion years to reach us

sources.label: NASA Science: Hubble gets the best image of bright quasar 3C 273

caveat: Observed, in NASA's rounded words (Hubble release of 21 Nov 2013). Apparent magnitude and redshift are not stated on the page, so none are given. 'Quasar' means a distant galaxy core powered by a supermassive black hole; NASA says the closest quasars are hundreds of millions of light-years away.

name: Io
summary: Moon of Jupiter and one of its four large Galilean moons.
distance: about 421,800 km from Jupiter (mean semi-major axis)
caveat: The orbit's size, shape and tilt are JPL mean elements; where the moon sits on its orbit on a given date is illustrative, because mean elements are not an ephemeris. Distances and sizes in the 3D view are compressed, and the surface is a generic artistic placeholder, not this moon's real appearance.
